input.instructions: Create a compact, accurate blueprint for an 8-to-12-minute educational lesson with exactly ten sequential teaching beats. Do not write full narration. Create exactly three measurable learning objectives. For every beat, provide one distinct complete factual claim, a concrete example, a concise editable visual direction, and one or two exact supplied source IDs. End the claim, example, and visual direction with complete punctuation. Every cited source excerpt must directly support the claim; reuse at least two important technical terms from each cited excerpt so support can be checked locally. Do not invent course assignments, policies, measurements, datasets, instruction encodings, or product behavior that is absent from the supplied excerpts. Keep the claim, example, and visual direction compact; a deterministic local expander will produce the full narration. Sequence the beats from foundations through application and end with a practical analysis checklist. Use only the supplied source excerpts for factual claims. Every factual claim must cite one or more supplied source IDs. Narration must describe information that is essential to understand visuals. Do not imitate a named creator or invent sources.
input.prompt:
Topic: CSCI-590: Undergraduate Thesis. This catalog entry has student-, instructor-, or term-specific content. Create a rigorous orientation companion that teaches the stable process, standards, planning methods, evaluation criteria, and representative examples without inventing a fixed RIT syllabus. Official catalog description: Thesis capstone of the Bachelor’s Degree Program. The thesis document identifies a central hypothesis or key problem(s), provides a critical review of related work, and reports methods, results, and conclusions from the associated research. Prerequisite: CSCI-589 or equivalent course. Contact Hours: Independent Study 1 Typically Offered: Fall, Spring, Summer

Source excerpts:

[acm-code-of-ethics]
The ACM Code directs computing professionals to contribute to society and human well-being. Computing professionals should avoid harm. They should be honest and trustworthy. They should be fair and take action not to discriminate. They should respect the work required to produce new ideas and creative works. They should respect privacy. They should honor confidentiality. Professionals should strive to achieve high quality in both processes and products. They should maintain high standards of professional competence, conduct, and ethical practice. Robust security should be designed and implemented when appropriate. Ethical computing decisions identify stakeholders, foreseeable benefits and harms, uncertainty, alternatives, and obligations.

[acm-research-practice]
Responsible technical communication distinguishes claims from evidence. It cites prior work and identifies the contribution being reported. Methods should be described well enough for readers to evaluate the work. Results should be reported accurately rather than selected to create a misleading conclusion. Limitations and threats to validity should be made visible. Authors should preserve research integrity and avoid plagiarism, fabrication, and falsification. Conflicts and relevant relationships should be disclosed according to publication policy. A research project narrows a question, reviews literature, defines a reproducible method, evaluates results, and communicates for the intended audience.

[rit-csci-590]
Thesis capstone of the Bachelor’s Degree Program. The thesis document identifies a central hypothesis or key problem(s), provides a critical review of related work, and reports methods, results, and conclusions from the associated research. Prerequisite: CSCI-589 or equivalent course. Contact Hours: Independent Study 1 Typically Offered: Fall, Spring, Summer

beats.claim: The thesis document identifies a central hypothesis or key problem(s), provides a critical review of related work, and reports methods, results, and conclusions from the associated
beats.example: A student formulates a hypothesis about algorithm efficiency, reviews prior papers, describes their experimental setup, reports performance metrics, and draws conclusions.
beats.title: Thesis Structure Overview
beats.visualDirection: Display a three-part diagram labeled 'Hypothesis', 'Review', and 'Methods/Results/Conclusions' with arrows showing sequential flow.

beats.claim: Students must complete CSCI-589 or an equivalent course before enrolling in this independent study.
beats.example: A student who finished CSCI-589: Advanced Algorithms can directly apply those foundational concepts to their thesis project.
beats.title: Prerequisite Alignment
beats.visualDirection: Show a simple prerequisite chain: 'CSCI-589 → CSCI-590' with a checkmark indicating readiness.

beats.claim: The course is structured as an independent study with one contact hour per term.
beats.example: Students schedule a single weekly meeting with their advisor to discuss progress, rather than attending full lecture sections.
beats.title: Independent Study Format
beats.visualDirection: Illustrate a calendar with one highlighted block labeled '1 Contact Hour' alongside a 'Self-Directed Research' badge.

beats.claim: The course is typically offered during Fall, Spring, and Summer terms.
beats.example: A student can enroll in the Fall term to complete research over the semester, or in the Summer term for a shorter, intensive cycle.
beats.title: Term Availability
beats.visualDirection: Display a timeline with three seasonal markers (Fall, Spring, Summer) and a 'Offered' tag next to each.

beats.claim: Responsible technical communication distinguishes claims from evidence and cites prior work.
beats.example: Instead of stating 'Our method is superior,' the student writes 'Our method reduces runtime by 15% compared to Baseline X, as shown in Table 3.'
beats.title: Responsible Communication Basics
beats.visualDirection: Show a side-by-side comparison: 'Claim' (bold, unsupported) vs. 'Evidence' (italic, cited, with data reference).

beats.claim: Methods should be described well enough for readers to evaluate the work.
beats.example: The student includes a reproducible protocol, specifying software versions, dataset sources, and exact parameter settings.
beats.title: Methods Documentation
beats.visualDirection: Display a checklist graphic with items: 'Reproducible Protocol', 'Software Versions', 'Dataset Sources', 'Parameter Settings'.

beats.claim: Results should be reported accurately rather than selected to create a misleading conclusion.
beats.example: The student presents all relevant metrics, including outliers, rather than editing data to fit a preferred narrative.
beats.title: Results Reporting Standards
beats.visualDirection: Show a bar chart with all data points visible, labeled 'Accurate Reporting', versus a cropped chart labeled 'Misleading Selection'.

beats.claim: Limitations and threats to validity should be made visible in the final document.
beats.example: The student explicitly states sample size constraints and environmental variables that may affect reproducibility.
beats.title: Limitations and Validity
beats.visualDirection: Illustrate a 'Limitations' section box with bullet points: 'Sample Size', 'Environmental Variables', 'Reproducibility Constraints'.

beats.claim: Authors should preserve research integrity and avoid plagiarism, fabrication, and falsification.
beats.example: The student uses citation managers to track sources and paraphrases text while maintaining proper attribution.
beats.title: Research Integrity Practices
beats.visualDirection: Show a flowchart: 'Original Idea → Cite Source → Paraphrase → Verify Attribution → Final Draft'.

beats.claim: Computing professionals should be honest, trustworthy, fair, and respect privacy and confidentiality.
beats.example: The student anonymizes participant data, avoids biased testing scenarios, and discloses any conflicts of interest.
beats.title: Ethical Computing Standards
beats.visualDirection: Display four ethical pillars: 'Honesty', 'Trustworthiness', 'Fairness', 'Privacy/Confidentiality' with icons.

Apply responsible technical communication principles by distinguishing claims from evidence and accurately reporting limitations.
Evaluate ethical and professional standards for research integrity, including confidentiality, fairness, and conflict disclosure.
